article-004.text: Which statement best summarises how the CDC describes ADHD?
options: It is a short-term behavioural phase that most children quickly outgrow.
It is a neurodevelopmental condition that can affect attention, activity and impulse control into adulthood.
It is caused primarily by parents setting inconsistent rules.
It is diagnosed whenever a child is occasionally restless.
article-004.evidence: ADHD is one of the most common neurodevelopmental disorders of childhood. It is usually first diagnosed in childhood and often lasts into adulthood.

article-004.text: How does predominantly inattentive ADHD differ from predominantly hyperactive-impulsive ADHD?
options: It mainly involves difficulty organising, focusing and following instructions, rather than restlessness and impulsivity.
It affects adults only, while hyperactive-impulsive ADHD affects children only.
It is always less severe and never affects schoolwork.
It is identified by increased physical activity rather than attention difficulties.
article-004.evidence: Predominantly Inattentive Presentation: It is hard for the individual to organize or finish a task, to pay attention to details, or to follow instructions or conversations.

article-004.text: What can reasonably be concluded from the discussion of ADHD causes?
options: Research has established excessive sugar intake as the leading cause.
ADHD is unrelated to genetic factors.
Environmental conditions have all been ruled out.
Genetics appears important, but the full range of causes and risk factors is not yet known.
article-004.evidence: The cause(s) and risk factors for ADHD are unknown, but current research shows that genetics plays an important role.

article-004.text: Why does the CDC recommend several steps when diagnosing ADHD?
options: Because symptoms must be present in every family member.
Because only a blood test can establish the condition.
Because other conditions can produce similar symptoms and there is no single definitive ADHD test.
Because parents' observations have no diagnostic value.
article-004.evidence: There is no single test to diagnose ADHD, and many other problems, like anxiety, depression, sleep problems, and certain types of learning disabilities, can have similar symptoms.

article-004.text: What approach is recommended first for preschool-aged children with ADHD?
options: Permanent removal from ordinary school settings.
Behaviour therapy, especially parent training, before trying medication.
Waiting until adulthood before seeking any support.
Medication without any follow-up or adjustment.
article-004.evidence: For preschool-aged children (4-5 years of age) with ADHD, behavior therapy, particularly training for parents, is recommended as the first line of treatment before medication is tried.

article-005.text: What central question does the writer explore by comparing Usain Bolt with the fictional Flash?
options: Whether fictional superheroes can train professional athletes.
Whether any sprinter has ever competed against a cheetah.
Whether there are biological limits to how fast humans can run.
Whether advanced running shoes can reverse ageing.
article-005.evidence: Is there a biological limit to how fast humans can run? Or will we all be sprinting like The Flash in future?

article-005.text: Why does Mark Denny consider it possible that Bolt's 100-metre record is close to the ultimate human limit?
options: His analysis of many racing records suggests performances tend to level off over time.
Every sport has already prohibited further training improvements.
Human muscles can contract without physical constraints.
Bolt's record was set before reliable timing technology existed.
article-005.evidence: Performances were clearly plateauing in all races

article-005.text: What distinction does the article make between four-legged sprinters and human runners?
options: Both are anatomically designed exclusively for long-distance endurance.
Humans are better suited to short bursts because their spines are more flexible.
Four-legged animals cannot reach high speeds without genetic engineering.
Animals such as cheetahs are built for short-term speed, whereas two-legged humans are better suited to endurance.
article-005.evidence: Four-legged animals like cheetahs – with their long legs, light body weight and flexible spine – are designed for short-term speed. Bipedal runners, meanwhile, are built for endurance.

article-005.text: Why would simply making a runner taller or giving them heavier bones not necessarily improve their maximum speed?
options: Height has no relationship of any kind to stride length.
Changes that could increase speed introduce limits or extra weight elsewhere in the body.
Increased height always eliminates muscle strength.
Longer legs prevent all movement at high speed.
article-005.evidence: Even if you made the bones more robust, they would then be heavier, negating what you’re trying to do.

article-005.text: What possibility does Denny suggest might allow future humans to move beyond their current biological speed limits?
options: Reaching the speed of light through ordinary sprint training.
Repeating the exact same training methods indefinitely.
Genetic engineering that changes muscle and body structures.
Replacing all competitive running with horse racing.
article-005.evidence: The only way you could go beyond these biological limits, says Denny, is with genetic engineering.

article-008.text: What is the interviewee's overall view of AI-generated art?
options: AI tools can assist artists, but genuine creativity and judgement remain primarily human.
AI has already developed human-like emotions and independent artistic opinions.
AI should replace artists because it never makes mistakes.
AI creativity no longer depends on the work of humans.
article-008.evidence: It’s a creative process that’s mainly human and AI is following the rules.

article-008.text: How do text-to-image AI models learn to connect a prompt with visual objects?
options: They rely entirely on a human to draw every requested image in real time.
They infer the meaning of words from captions paired with large numbers of training images.
They are programmed with a complete dictionary of every possible scene.
They automatically verify all images against objective truth before training.
article-008.evidence: This worked by training the model on lots of images and their accompanying text caption to understand how the words relate to the images.

article-008.text: Why are generative image models especially prone to mistakes in small details such as hands?
options: Human viewers are generally unable to notice such mistakes.
The systems deliberately refuse to generate human anatomy.
Small details are absent from all their training pictures.
Their optimisation prioritises getting the overall image right rather than every small feature.
article-008.evidence: The AI neglects the small details that we, as humans, are tuned to catch – a hand with four fingers or a three-legged person, for example.

article-008.text: What makes training large image-generation systems environmentally costly?
options: Most images have to be physically printed before they can be used.
The models can run only on devices powered by fossil fuels.
They require extensive processing on energy-consuming GPUs over long periods.
The interview claims digital images use no electricity during training.
article-008.evidence: The training process for these models requires a lot of energy. You need to run them on graphical processing units (GPUs) for weeks while they process billions of images.

article-008.text: What is the interviewee's main concern about the way current image models are trained?
options: They use large numbers of artists' internet images without obtaining the artists' consent.
They learn exclusively from photographs owned by the person using the tool.
They have completely solved questions of artistic ownership.
All training images are made by the model without any human source material.
article-008.evidence: The copyright issue comes with the use of millions of images taken from the internet without consent of the artist.

article-040.text: What central problem does Christopher Reddy believe scientists must address?
options: They should withdraw completely from public debate.
Researchers should explain their work more clearly to non-specialists during crises.
Scientific research should stop whenever the public disagrees.
The media should replace scientists in explaining technical evidence.
article-040.evidence: The core problem is rooted in academia itself: communication with non-scientists is not appreciated

article-040.text: What did Reddy learn from his early research on oil spills?
options: The research had no practical use in disasters.
Government agencies always apply new evidence immediately.
The public can understand only research published in academic journals.
Useful scientific findings may be ignored when researchers do not communicate with those who need them.
article-040.evidence: industry and cleanup specialists rarely paid attention to the developing science, in part because researchers like him were not talking to those who might make use of their work.

article-040.text: How do the expectations of the public and scientists differ during a crisis, according to Reddy?
options: Scientists may accept prolonged uncertainty, while members of the public often want immediate clear answers.
Both groups expect every complex research problem to be solved within seconds.
The public generally welcomes years of uncertainty more than researchers do.
Scientists prefer instant certainty and avoid examining evidence.
article-040.evidence: A scientist is more than willing to wait weeks, months, years, even decades to solve an outstanding research question. The public wants certainty, and they want it in four seconds.

article-040.text: Why might scientists hesitate to offer a clear explanation in public?
options: They are legally forbidden to speak about their studies.
They believe scientific accuracy requires never speaking to journalists.
They fear professional criticism or lasting damage to their reputations if they make a mistake.
They think journalists always understand uncertainty better than specialists.
article-040.evidence: When you venture outside of the ivory tower and make a mistake, more often than not the risk is greater than the reward

article-040.text: Why does the article discuss the Deepwater Horizon oil spill?
options: To argue that environmental research should end after a disaster.
To illustrate how scientific expertise can be crucial yet poorly understood or communicated during an emergency.
To prove that oil spills pose no environmental risks.
To show that every disagreement between the media and researchers was resolved instantly.
article-040.evidence: Initial containment, damage assessment and environmental restoration work all hinged on our contributions.

article-006.text: Why are the carvings at La Roche-Cotard cave significant to archaeologists?
options: They prove that modern humans invented all European cave art.
They may be among the earliest surviving examples of art made by Neanderthals.
They show that early Europeans used written alphabets.
They reveal that Neanderthals lived exclusively in caves.
article-006.evidence: The engravings are some of the oldest known examples of Neanderthal art and are possibly the very oldest.

article-006.text: What combination of evidence supports the attribution of the cave markings to Neanderthals?
options: Modern human skeletons and Roman coins found in the chamber.
Written records left by the cave's occupants.
The absence of any stone tools and evidence of modern habitation.
Mousterian tools associated with Neanderthals and the ancient sealing of the cave entrance.
article-006.evidence: The attribution of the engravings to Neanderthals, not modern humans, rests partly on the distinctive Mousterian tools found in the cave and partly on the timing.

article-006.text: What does the article indicate about the meaning of the engravings?
options: Researchers cannot yet confidently establish whether they had a shared symbolic meaning.
Each marking has been translated as a specific word.
They were definitely maps of Neanderthal hunting grounds.
Their purpose is known from accompanying written inscriptions.
article-006.evidence: It isn’t clear whether the engravings “represent symbolic thinking”

article-006.text: How does April Nowell distinguish this evidence from the art associated with Homo sapiens?
options: Neanderthal engravings always contain longer repeated sequences.
There is no evidence that modern humans produced symbolic objects.
The Neanderthal examples appear relatively isolated, unlike more frequent recurring elements in H. sapiens art.
Both traditions are known only from a single cave.
article-006.evidence: There are no other known Neanderthal sites with engravings like those in La Roche-Cotard or Gorham’s cave – whereas prehistoric art by H. sapiens is more common and contains repeating elements.

article-006.text: What possibility does Paola Villa raise about symbolic behaviour?
options: Neanderthals learned all symbolism from medieval people.
Modern humans may have learned or developed some symbolic behaviours through contact with Neanderthals.
Both populations remained completely isolated from one another.
Symbolic behaviour disappeared as soon as modern humans arrived.
article-006.evidence: It may be that modern humans picked up some symbolic Neanderthal behaviours and developed them, says Villa.

article-007.text: What does the author argue about people's ability to recognise liars?
options: Ordinary people are consistently accurate when reading facial expressions.
Body language provides a scientifically reliable lie detector.
Even deliberate deception can be difficult to identify, despite popular beliefs about telltale behaviour.
The ability to spot lies depends solely on the listener's education.
article-007.evidence: The weight of empirical research shows it’s hard to identify even very purposeful liars from their behaviour.

article-007.text: What does the 2006 meta-analysis of deception judgments suggest?
options: People's ability to distinguish lies from truths is only slightly better than chance.
Most people identify deception correctly in virtually every case.
People become accurate lie detectors after hearing one convincing story.
The analysis found that liars share one unmistakable physical gesture.
article-007.evidence: looked at more than 200 studies to find that people’s accuracy when distinguishing truth from lies isn’t much better than chance.

article-007.text: Why might a charming friend be especially convincing when telling an implausible story?
options: Close friends usually provide independent proof for all their claims.
Attractive people cannot deliberately lie to people they know.
A friend's physical appearance always reveals whether they are dishonest.
Trust and intimacy may lower the listener's guard and make the friend's account easier to accept.
article-007.evidence: The flipside of heightened intimacy is lowered guards.

article-007.text: What is the purpose of the author's account of the woman called Julia?
options: To show that lies occur only between strangers.
To illustrate how an apparently caring person's false claims can undermine others' trust in their perceptions.
To prove that Julia's claims were confirmed by independent investigators.
To suggest that everybody knowingly accepts dishonesty in their relationships.
article-007.evidence: Over time my trust in my judgment eroded.

article-007.text: Which conclusion best follows from the article's discussion of deceptive behaviour?
options: The listener's assumptions and relationship with the speaker can influence whether a lie is believed.
A person's posture alone is sufficient to establish the truth.
A liar who believes their story will always confess immediately.
Empirical research proves that every deceptive person looks away while speaking.
article-007.evidence: People who convince themselves of their own truthfulness while being dishonest may act no differently to normal.

article-009.text: What is the article's overall position on the fall of the Roman Empire?
options: Rome ended on a single date for one universally accepted reason.
Its decline was a complex process involving multiple causes, and even the idea of a straightforward 'fall' is debated.
The empire ended only because it expanded into North Africa.
All scholars agree that the empire survived unchanged.
article-009.evidence: Just as the Fall of Rome was not caused by a single event, the way Rome fell was also complex.

article-009.text: Why is identifying one precise date for Rome's fall problematic?
options: No Roman historical records have survived.
The Roman Empire existed for less than a decade.
The city of Rome never served as an imperial centre.
Changes occurred over a long period and the empire's political and geographic structure altered.
article-009.evidence: In fact, during the period of imperial decline, the empire actually expanded.

article-009.text: What political change did the division between East and West bring?
options: Every province immediately became an independent state.
Rome permanently became the capital of both halves.
New imperial centres developed, including Constantinople in the East and Milan in the West.
The Roman army was abolished throughout the empire.
article-009.evidence: The schism of east and west created not just an eastern capital first in Nicomedia and then Constantinople, but also a move in the west from Rome to Milan.

article-009.text: What role does Christianity play in one interpretation of Rome's decline?
options: Growing church influence and new religious allegiances could conflict with existing imperial authority and traditions.
Christianity was the established state religion throughout the empire's entire history.
Church leaders always supported the deification of emperors.
Religion is ruled out as a relevant factor by every historian quoted.
article-009.evidence: Over time, Christian church leaders became increasingly influential, eroding the emperors' powers.

article-009.text: How does the account complicate the portrayal of outsiders as merely enemies of Rome?
options: Outsiders never entered imperial territory.
They contributed soldiers and revenue to Rome even as the empire later lost territory and resources to some of them.
They supplied Rome with no military personnel or taxes.
All groups described as barbarians acted in exactly the same way.
article-009.evidence: The barbarians, which is a term that covers a varied and changing group of outsiders, were embraced by Rome, who used them as suppliers of tax revenue and bodies for the military

article-010.text: How does the article describe the development of mental strength?
options: As a fixed trait that cannot change after childhood.
As an automatic result of professional success.
As something that depends mainly on avoiding difficulties.
As a capacity strengthened through deliberate practice and everyday habits.
article-010.evidence: cultivating mental strength isn’t automatic. Instead, it demands regular exercise and mindful practice

article-010.text: Why does the writer recommend regular self-reflection?
options: To avoid having to make decisions independently.
To better recognise emotions, motivations and responses, and learn from past experiences.
To remove the need to interact with other people.
To ensure that every decision is free from uncertainty.
article-010.evidence: This practice offers opportunities to analyze past actions, learn from successes and failures, and gain insights into how they might improve.

article-010.text: What attitude towards change characterises mentally strong individuals in the article?
options: They resist every unfamiliar situation regardless of the consequences.
They expect their plans never to require adjustment.
They treat new circumstances as potential opportunities and adapt their plans when necessary.
They see adaptability as a sign that their goals do not matter.
article-010.evidence: They view change not as a threat but as an opportunity for growth.

article-010.text: What does the author's discussion of persistence imply about failure?
options: Setbacks can provide lessons rather than marking the end of progress.
Strong people avoid all situations in which they might fail.
Achieving a goal requires never changing an ineffective approach.
People should immediately abandon goals when they meet resistance.
article-010.evidence: They understand that setbacks and failures form part of the journey and serve as vital learning opportunities.

article-010.text: How does the writer distinguish optimism from ignoring problems?
options: Optimism requires pretending that challenges do not exist.
Optimism removes the need for rest or self-care.
A positive attitude can be maintained only when life is easy.
Optimism involves recognising difficulties while focusing on constructive possibilities.
article-010.evidence: Positivity is not about ignoring the difficulties of life. Instead, it involves acknowledging challenges and focusing on the bright side of situations.

article-011.text: What is the article's central argument about why food tastes delicious?
options: It depends entirely on the number of taste buds a person has.
It results exclusively from the food's chemical composition.
Flavour emerges from sensory signals together with experience, expectations and context.
It is determined before birth and cannot be influenced by learning.
article-011.evidence: our biases filter the taste experience

article-011.text: What does the discovery of taste receptors outside the mouth suggest?
options: Taste-related biology is more complex and widespread than the traditional tongue-only account.
The mouth plays no role in how food is experienced.
Taste receptors work only when people are asleep.
The discovery proves that personal preferences are identical for everyone.
article-011.evidence: scientists have found taste receptors all over the body

article-011.text: Why does the writer distinguish the physiology of flavour from what people like to eat?
options: Because the body's digestive system operates independently of the brain.
Because understanding sensory mechanisms alone does not explain individual food preferences.
Because food preferences cannot change at any age.
Because taste can be explained only through genetics.
article-011.evidence: This physiology may explain what we mean by flavor—but anatomy doesn't much help us understand what we like.

article-011.text: What does the example involving researchers, food pictures and mild electrical stimulation illustrate?
options: Food preference depends exclusively on the temperature of the tongue.
Electricity can permanently replace every taste receptor.
People can accurately identify flavours without any sensory input.
Expectations and other sensory cues can influence how taste is experienced.
article-011.evidence: researchers connected volunteers' tongues to a low-voltage electrical device, showed them pictures of food items

article-011.text: Which conclusion best reflects the writer's discussion of deliciousness?
options: A meal's social and personal setting may shape its perceived flavour.
A food's appeal is fixed by its nutritional content alone.
People's childhood experiences have no connection with taste.
Taste preferences are fully explained by anatomy.
article-011.evidence: Deliciousness comes from our mother, our childhood, the room we are eating in, the plates we are eating on and the friends

article-012.text: Which claim does the neuroscience columnist principally seek to challenge?
options: That sleep influences memory formation.
That humans normally use only 10 per cent of their brains.
That the brain requires energy to function.
That scientific findings can be misunderstood.
article-012.evidence: THE IDEA THAT WE ONLY USE 10 PER CENT OF OUR BRAINS IS A MYTH THAT NEEDS TO DIE

article-012.text: Why does the author compare an underused brain to a supercomputer used only as a clock?
options: To argue that brains literally operate like car computers.
To suggest that the brain has no specialised functions.
To illustrate how implausibly wasteful it would be to maintain such an expensive organ while using almost none of it.
To claim technology can replace the human brain.
article-012.evidence: having a brain as biologically demanding as ours but only using 10 per cent of it, is like bolting a giant supercomputer onto your sports car just to set the clock

article-012.text: According to the writer, why can the 10-per-cent myth be harmful?
options: It provides an apparent justification for unfounded claims about untapped brain powers.
It causes the brain to stop processing visual information.
It has conclusively disproved modern neuroscience.
It makes all brain training scientifically impossible.
article-012.evidence: the ‘we only use 10 per cent of our brain’ myth provides a huge ‘unknown’ space in which pseudoscientific/bogus brain-based claims can hide

article-012.text: What does the discussion of the myth's possible origins suggest?
options: Its exact inventor has been identified beyond dispute.
It was invented only after magnetic brain scanning became widespread.
It has been disproved only in the past few months.
Its precise origins are uncertain, but the idea has circulated for well over a century.
article-012.evidence: even though the true origins of the myth remain unclear, one thing we can say for certain is that they go back a long way

article-012.text: What broader lesson does the writer draw from the persistence of the myth?
options: Modern research should never revise earlier ideas.
Old or incomplete findings should not be turned into sweeping claims about how the brain works.
Scientific understanding remains unchanged for centuries.
Misconceptions disappear automatically when evidence improves.
article-012.evidence: the dangers of forming blanket conclusions based on very old research

article-013.text: What is the main theme of the readers' responses to the question about a person who has never suffered?
options: The importance of eliminating every ordinary frustration.
The certainty that hardship always improves character.
The difficulty of predicting personality without adversity, because people learn and respond differently.
The claim that empathy is a purely inherited trait.
article-013.evidence: The few who have experienced none of this could be functional, successful, happy, but could also be oblivious, entitled and judgmental.

article-013.text: What does the example of the child upset by a stolen ice cream suggest?
options: Experiences that seem minor to others may still feel intensely distressing to an individual.
Only adults can recognise emotional distress.
Any disappointment is necessarily traumatic.
Children who have stable lives are never disappointed.
article-013.evidence: when a seagull stole her ice- cream, she screamed and burst into tears

article-013.text: Why do some contributors warn against assuming that a hardship-free person would be automatically kind?
options: They believe empathy can arise only from severe injury.
They argue that happiness is incompatible with moral behaviour.
They assume everyone who is wealthy lacks sympathy.
Without perspective on others' difficulties, someone might become entitled or judgmental.
article-013.evidence: if they decided that bad things must only happen to bad people, or they’re somehow above everyone else’s problems

article-013.text: What conclusion follows from the claim that two people can experience the same event differently?
options: Trauma depends only on the event's public seriousness.
Individual reactions to difficult experiences differ rather than following one universal pattern.
Every adverse experience produces identical long-term effects.
No one can be harmed by experiences shared with others.
article-013.evidence: two people could have the exact same experience and one of them be traumatised and the other not

article-013.text: How does the discussion of stories and fiction complicate the original thought experiment?
options: It suggests that people can acquire emotional understanding indirectly through others' experiences.
It proves that fiction prevents people from feeling pain.
It treats personal experience as the only source of empathy.
It argues that books can replace all social relationships.

article-014.text: What is the article primarily reporting about The Simpsons and the missing submersible?
options: The show directly assisted the Coast Guard's investigation.
The show's writers had received confidential information about the voyage.
Fans noticed apparent similarities between an older fictional episode and a real maritime emergency.
The cartoon caused the submersible's navigation system to fail.
article-014.evidence: ‘The Simpsons’ fans say show predicted Titanic submarine disappearance 17 years ago

article-014.text: Why did viewers connect a previous Simpsons story with the Titan incident?
options: The episode had already documented the real passenger list.
A fictional underwater exploration scene resembled elements of the later search for the missing vessel.
The programme had been filmed on board the real vessel.
The animation contained an official Coast Guard report.
article-014.evidence: After exploring for a bit, the duo comes across the remains of a massive ship filled to the brim with treasure.

article-014.text: According to the report, what made the search for the submersible urgent?
options: The vessel had been missing for years.
Its passengers were known to be safely ashore.
The submersible was carrying hazardous radioactive material.
Five people were aboard and contact was lost during a deep-water dive.
article-014.evidence: lost contact with the crew about an hour and 45 minutes into the dive

article-014.text: How should the social media comments about the writers' supposed prediction be understood?
options: As reactions from fans rather than proof that the writers knew future events.
As verified evidence of advance knowledge held by the show's producers.
As official statements by maritime safety investigators.
As scientific findings about predicting accidents.
article-014.evidence: The Simpson writers should be investigated because this is insane

article-014.text: What additional concern about submersible safety appears in the report?
options: The vessel was required to use only renewable fuel.
Criticism had been raised about inadequate non-destructive testing of the hull.
The crew had been ordered not to communicate with surface vessels.
Every component had passed all possible independent safety checks.
article-014.evidence: lack of non-destructive testing performed on the hull of the Titan

article-015.text: What conclusion did the Coast Guard draw from the debris found in the North Atlantic?
options: The missing vessel had safely reached the Titanic wreck.
The reported underwater noises were definitely produced by the passengers.
The evidence indicated that the submersible had suffered a catastrophic implosion.
The submersible was still transmitting from beneath the surface.
article-015.evidence: a debris field located in the North Atlantic suggests that a submersible missing since Sunday, with five passengers on board, suffered a "catastrophic implosion"

article-015.text: Why were the underwater noises reported during the search initially significant?
options: They offered a possible lead, although investigators could not establish that they came from the missing vessel.
They confirmed that the passengers had safely left the submersible.
They were identified as messages sent by the vessel's onboard radio.
They immediately revealed the precise location of the wreck.
article-015.evidence: hopes were raised when a Canadian plane picked up underwater noises, but the US Coast Guard was unable to confirm they were from the sub

article-015.text: What happened when remotely operated vehicles were moved to investigate the reported sounds?
options: They recovered all passengers alive.
They successfully located the source of each noise.
They were withdrawn before reaching the search zone.
Their search did not produce a positive result.
article-015.evidence: ROV operations had been relocated "in an attempt to explore the origin of the noises", but "yielded negative results"

article-015.text: What does the article's account of the loss of contact suggest about the search operation?
options: The vessel was tracked continuously during the entire descent.
The incident became apparent only after communications stopped during the descent and the vessel failed to return as expected.
Authorities had confirmed the incident before the dive began.
No search coordination was needed because the vessel resurfaced on time.
article-015.evidence: Contact was lost one hour and 45 minutes into its descent

article-015.text: Which statement best describes the eventual search response?
options: The search expanded indefinitely with all rescue craft remaining deployed.
Investigators concluded that debris provided no useful information.
The main search began winding down while remotely operated vehicles remained at the site.
The Coast Guard immediately abandoned all underwater examination.
article-015.evidence: The search is being wound down over the next 24 hours, although remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) will remain on site.

article-016.text: What is the writer's overall position on social media and teenage mental health?
options: Social media is uniformly beneficial for teenagers.
Online platforms have no measurable association with wellbeing.
Social media offers potential benefits but can also pose significant mental-health risks.
All teenagers should be completely barred from online communication.
article-016.evidence: The ultimate goal should be to harness the potential benefits of online social connections, while decreasing the potential harms.

article-016.text: What did the study mentioned in the article associate with using social media for more than three hours a day?
options: A heightened risk of problems including depression and anxiety symptoms.
Guaranteed long-term improvement in mental health.
The disappearance of anxiety among young people.
A reduction in sleep needs for all teenagers.
article-016.evidence: those who spent more than 3 hours per day on social media platforms were at heightened risk of mental health problems

article-016.text: Why does the writer cite a survey finding that US 15-to-16-year-olds averaged 3.5 hours a day on social media?
options: To prove that only adults face online harms.
To show that the level of use linked to risk is not uncommon among teenagers.
To establish that exactly three hours is medically safe for everyone.
To argue that adolescents no longer use face-to-face communication.
article-016.evidence: 15 to 16-year-olds in the US spent an average of 3.5 hours on social media per day

article-016.text: What important uncertainty does the writer identify about social media use and mental-health problems?
options: Whether computers require an internet connection.
Whether students use platforms for homework.
Whether screen time can be measured reliably.
The relationship may work in both directions rather than simply causing harm in one direction.
article-016.evidence: It willbe important to understand the two-way nature of associations between social media use and mental health issues

article-016.text: What practical goal follows from the article's balanced perspective?
options: Preserve opportunities for online connection while finding ways to reduce associated risks.
Treat all digital communication as useless.
Ignore any reported mental-health symptoms.
Assume that online socialising always has the same effects regardless of use.
article-016.evidence: harness the potential benefits of online social connections, while decreasing the potential harms

article-017.text: What is the main criticism of Britain's ambition to become an AI superpower?
options: The country has already built more advanced computing facilities than it needs.
The government should avoid all investment in artificial intelligence.
Political enthusiasm is not yet matched by sufficient computing infrastructure and practical strategy.
Britain's universities have no interest in researching AI.
article-017.evidence: Rishi Sunak’s enthusiasm is welcome. But his plans to make Britain into an AI superpower fall short

article-017.text: Why is access to advanced graphics processing units important in the article's argument?
options: GPUs are mainly used to print paper research reports.
Large AI models need substantial specialised computing resources for training.
They make data and software unnecessary.
AI research depends exclusively on government speeches.
article-017.evidence: advanced graphics processing units (GPUs) needed to train large models

article-017.text: What problem does the author see in Britain's position as a location for large-scale AI computation?
options: All global cloud firms have already moved their main systems to Britain.
Advanced computing cannot operate outside the United States.
Britain has prohibited the import of graphics hardware.
Despite some existing capacity, major cloud providers have not committed Britain as a key location for frontier computing.
article-017.evidence: none of the cloud­computing giants has yet chosen Britain as the base for what techies call the “compute”

article-017.text: What is implied by the writer's call for more engineers in government?
options: AI policies need people who understand the practical interplay of data, hardware and model development.
Only civil servants with law degrees should oversee technology.
Government decisions can safely ignore technical constraints.
Engineering expertise has no role in regulation.
article-017.evidence: his gov­ ernment should include more engineers who understand the mix of data and compute from which AI is built

article-017.text: What is the significance of encouraging competing chipmakers?
options: It would eliminate the need for any programming software.
It would ensure only one supplier controls AI computing.
Better software support could help rivals challenge the dominant provider and ease hardware shortages.
It would prevent researchers from sharing new models.
article-017.evidence: With better software their chips could compete with Nvidia’s and ease the supply crunch

article-018.text: What central connection does the author make between air pollution and climate action?
options: Toxic air is solely an aesthetic problem in cities.
Reducing air pollution can protect public health while helping tackle the climate emergency.
Air pollution has already ceased to pose a risk.
Climate action has no effect on the air people breathe.
article-018.evidence: Tackling our toxic air is crucial, not just for good health, but as a means to confront the climate crisis

article-018.text: Why does the author refer to Rosamund Kissi-Debrah?
options: To show how personal experiences of the harm caused by dirty air can motivate urgent public action.
To argue that city transport is unrelated to health.
To claim no parents have raised concerns about pollution.
To suggest that individual campaigners cannot influence policy debates.
article-018.evidence: Rosamund has continually emphasised the need to do more, and faster, on air pollution

article-018.text: What does the World Health Organization statistic about global air quality support?
options: Only a small number of cities need to consider air pollution.
Air pollution is limited to industrial work sites.
Air pollution is a widespread public-health problem rather than a rare local concern.
Most people worldwide breathe air entirely free from pollutants.
article-018.evidence: 99 per cent of the global population breathe toxic air

article-018.text: Why does the writer mention thousands of premature deaths in London?
options: To show that urban population growth has stopped.
To explain why London has no transport network.
To argue that mortality is unrelated to environmental conditions.
To emphasise that toxic air has serious, measurable human consequences even within one city.
article-018.evidence: in London alone, around 4000 people die prematurely each year because of toxic air

article-018.text: What wider lesson does the writer take from his contact with air-pollution campaigners?
options: Climate and public-health problems should always be treated as unrelated.
The climate emergency should also be understood as a health emergency.
Climate change has no local consequences for residents.
Policies should focus on short-term convenience and set aside medical evidence.
article-018.evidence: She taught me that we aren’t just in a climate crisis, but a health one too.

article-019.text: What apparent contradiction forms the article's main theme?
options: People can admire the image of gangsters despite acknowledging the harm and illegality of their actions.
Most gangsters have entirely legitimate careers.
Crime is considered socially harmless in all cultures.
Gangsters are universally rejected in popular culture.
article-019.evidence: even though most people would disagree with the illegal activities that gangsters participate in, many can’t help but hold a grudging respect

article-019.text: Why does the writer discuss gangsters who rose from poverty?
options: To claim that crime is the only way to become wealthy.
To prove that gangsters are better leaders than elected officials.
To explain how stories of self-made success can make criminals appealing to some admirers.
To show that financial background plays no role in romanticisation.
article-019.evidence: started out with nothing, but ended up some of the most wealthy criminals in history

article-019.text: How does the notion of power fantasies help explain the appeal of gangsters?
options: Admiration is entirely based on an accurate understanding of criminal law.
Imagined freedom to defy social rules can fascinate people even if they would reject those acts in reality.
People idolise gangsters only for their charitable donations.
Every admirer intends to commit violent crimes.
article-019.evidence: the idea of being able to commit taboo crimes like arson and murder is still appealing to many as a power fantasy

article-019.text: What is the role of wealth and luxury in the image the article describes?
options: They make gangsters universally respected by police.
They prove that illegal behaviour has no financial rewards.
They are dismissed as irrelevant to popular portrayals.
They can create an attractive image that distracts some observers from the damage caused by criminal activity.
article-019.evidence: Along with the lavish lifestyle, another reason many people idolize gangsters is the money they make.

article-019.text: Why does the article characterise gangsters as anti-heroes?
options: They combine morally objectionable actions with qualities or narratives that some people still find compelling.
They are always depicted as innocent victims of society.
They avoid rule-breaking as a matter of principle.
They are admired only because viewers believe no crimes occurred.
article-019.evidence: Gangsters Are Anti-Heroes Even though most people would disagree with the illegal activities

article-020.text: What is the main point of the review of The Limits of Genius?
options: Brilliant thinkers never make impractical decisions.
Some highly intelligent people still behave foolishly and make avoidable mistakes.
Scientific discovery depends entirely on reckless conduct.
Unusual behaviour is proof that someone lacks intelligence.
article-020.evidence: Being a genius won’t stop you staring at an eclipse or letting an argument keep you from finding a planet

article-020.text: Why does the reviewer mention Isaac Newton and Donald Trump in the same discussion?
options: To establish that they shared identical careers in science.
To explain a family relationship between them.
To contrast their scientific achievements in detail.
To illustrate that very different public figures can exhibit similarly ill-advised behaviour.
article-020.evidence: Mathematician and science writer Katie Spalding says that both were stupid enough to stare directly at the sun.

article-020.text: What does the account of staring directly at the Sun demonstrate?
options: High intelligence does not prevent a person from taking an obviously dangerous action.
Direct sunlight is always safe when viewed with optical equipment.
Scientists had no knowledge of eye injuries in earlier centuries.
Visual damage cannot follow from risky experiments.
article-020.evidence: he had trouble for months afterwards

article-020.text: What larger argument does the book make through humorous historical examples?
options: Every major discovery was made by accident alone.
Scientific progress requires that researchers refuse advice.
Intellectual achievement does not guarantee consistently sound judgment.
People with scientific training are unable to recognise errors.
article-020.evidence: Being a genius won’t stop you staring at an eclipse

article-020.text: How does the reviewer describe the author's treatment of her subjects?
options: As a technical manual with no reference to personalities.
As an engaging account that relishes oddities and amusing mistakes alongside achievement.
As evidence that all past scientists were deliberately dishonest.
As an argument that research should end whenever errors occur.
article-020.evidence: She also relishes the silly footnote

article-021.text: What makes temporarily exceeding 1.5°C of global warming significant in the article?
options: It would mean that the world's climate had returned to pre-industrial conditions.
It would mark an important threshold even if daily life initially continued much as before.
It would immediately end all forms of economic activity.
It would prove that climate change cannot affect human society.
article-021.evidence: make 2024 the year that global warming exceeds 1.5°C for the first time

article-021.text: How does the author expect extreme weather to change as temperatures increase?
options: Heatwaves, droughts, wildfires and heavy rainfall are likely to intensify.
All regions will receive exactly the same amount of rain.
Extreme weather will gradually disappear from temperate climates.
Only daytime temperatures will change; rainfall will remain constant.
article-021.evidence: Heatwaves will be fiercer, droughts longer, wildfires more frequent and rainstorms heavier

article-021.text: Why does the writer discuss Arctic communities and traditional culture?
options: To argue that Arctic regions are unaffected by rising temperatures.
To suggest that climate change is a problem only for tourism.
To demonstrate that climate change can affect social wellbeing and ways of life, not just weather records.
To show that every Arctic community has already relocated permanently.
article-021.evidence: climate change is having a profound effect on the traditional culture and well-being of communities

article-021.text: What does the discussion of Pacific island communities illustrate?
options: Coastal societies face no risk from rising seas.
Migration always solves the causes of climate change.
Future climate effects cannot alter where people live.
Climate impacts may force displacement and threaten people's ability to remain in their homes.
article-021.evidence: Climate displacement of populations is the main feature of our future

article-021.text: What conclusion does the article draw about exceeding the 1.5°C target?
options: A temporary overshoot removes the need for emissions cuts.
Returning temperatures to the target may remain possible, but becomes harder the further warming exceeds it.
Any warming above 1.5°C can be reversed instantly.
Climate change can be stopped without changing greenhouse-gas emissions.
article-021.evidence: But the more we overshoot, the harder it will be to get back.

article-022.text: What does the article suggest about the often-repeated target of 10,000 daily steps?
options: It is the minimum required for any health benefit.
People receive no benefit if they walk fewer steps.
It can be a useful goal, but health benefits do not depend on reaching it every day.
It is a medical prescription that suits every age and ability.
article-022.evidence: you don’t need to hit that number every time for your steps to 'count'

article-022.text: Why does the trainer advise against a one-size-fits-all walking target?
options: People's circumstances and fitness goals vary, so regular movement matters more than a rigid universal number.
Walking helps only people who already exercise intensely.
Exercise requirements can be determined solely by body height.
Everyone needs exactly the same pace to stay healthy.
article-022.evidence: Because we are all different, our fitness goals won't be 'one-size-fits-all.'

article-022.text: How does the article recommend fitting walking into a working day?
options: By avoiding all movement until after work.
By setting aside brief breaks to walk between tasks.
By replacing every work meeting with an intense workout.
By waiting until the weekend to accumulate all steps.
article-022.evidence: schedule five to ten- minute breaks to take short walks between tasks at work

article-022.text: What do the examples of household chores and walking the dog illustrate?
options: Chores prevent people from exercising outdoors.
Fitness trackers must be used for every movement.
Walking is beneficial only when done in a gym.
Everyday routines can provide opportunities to accumulate movement without a dedicated workout.
article-022.evidence: Cleaning up after dinner, walking the dog, taking the trash out, folding laundry and unloading the dishwasher

article-022.text: Why does the writer recommend treating walking as part of a lifestyle?
options: Because walking becomes useless once a numerical target is reached.
Because the purpose of walking is to satisfy a device's daily score.
Because an ongoing habit is more sustainable than simply ticking off an isolated task.
Because occasional exercise is always harmful.
article-022.evidence: Consider walking as a part of your lifestyle rather than as a task to check off your list

article-023.text: What broader benefit of language learning does the article emphasise beyond communication?
options: It helps learners understand other cultures and perspectives.
It guarantees higher salaries to every learner.
It removes the need to interact with native speakers.
It prevents people from making mistakes in their first language.
article-023.evidence: Learning a new language can give you another perspective or insight into a culture and mindset.

article-023.text: What does the discussion of adults and mistakes imply about learning a language?
options: Adults are biologically incapable of acquiring new languages.
Adults always learn faster by avoiding conversation.
Excessive fear of mistakes may hold learners back, so willingness to practise is valuable.
Making an error proves that the learning method has failed.
article-023.evidence: Adults tend to mull over every mistake

article-023.text: Why does the article support using the target language during lessons?
options: It makes classroom feedback unnecessary.
It creates meaningful practice and exposure rather than limiting learning to theory.
It ensures that every word is immediately memorised.
It prevents learners from understanding any grammar.
article-023.evidence: A teacher’s adamance for you to only speak that foreign language in the classroom

article-023.text: What is the educational value of songs mentioned in the article?
options: They make grammar study permanently unnecessary.
They work only for people who can sing professionally.
They provide no language input beyond entertainment.
They offer a more engaging way to practise and break up repetitive study.
article-023.evidence: Songs are a great way to break up the monotony of regular studying.

article-023.text: Which approach is most consistent with the article's final practical advice?
options: Focus on real messages and early communication rather than waiting to master every isolated rule.
Avoid listening until you have memorised a full dictionary.
Use translations only and never attempt original sentences.
Delay speaking until grammatical accuracy is perfect.
article-023.evidence: Start learning a new language to communicate from day one

article-024.text: Which contrast does the article make between 'agentic' and 'communal' first-impression behaviours?
options: Agentic behaviour is always preferred for deep relationships.
People may appreciate confidence, but warm and responsive communal behaviour is especially important for forming closer connections.
Neither kind of behaviour has any effect on how strangers respond.
Communal behaviour is described as avoiding emotional expression.
article-024.evidence: participants preferred those who engaged in more communal behavior when it came to whether the person was interested in making a deeper connection

article-024.text: Why does the writer emphasise being receptive to other people?
options: To encourage strangers to compete for attention.
To show that first impressions cannot be influenced.
Because responsiveness and kindness can make someone seem more approachable and likeable.
Because conversations should be controlled by only one person.
article-024.evidence: Being kind, emotionally expressive, and receptive to the other person leads to more likability.

article-024.text: What does the research described imply about making a lasting social connection?
options: Warmth and communal qualities may matter more than appearing assertive alone.
An aggressive personality is always required.
Physical appearance is the only determinant.
People always prefer identical traits regardless of context.
article-024.evidence: For more long-term and deeper connections, however, most prefer those who display communal behaviors.

article-024.text: How does the article qualify its findings about social preferences?
options: It claims people never differ in whom they find appealing.
It denies that non-verbal behaviour affects impressions.
It says every participant had the same response.
It acknowledges that individuals differ and some are drawn to more agentic behaviour.
article-024.evidence: there are always individual differences, as some prefer the more “agentic types.”

article-024.text: What role does body language play in the article's discussion?
options: Positive non-verbal signals can encourage others to want to know a person better.
Body language proves whether someone is morally good.
Facial expression has no connection with interaction.
Any display of confidence is automatically disliked.
article-024.evidence: Positive body language makes people want to get to know you

article-025.text: What does the example of elephants shrinking and rats growing on an island illustrate?
options: Evolution always makes all animals smaller.
Isolated island conditions can favour different changes in the body sizes of large and small animals.
Animals stop evolving once they reach an island.
Only mammals experience evolutionary change.
article-025.evidence: the elephants shrink to the size of Shetland ponies and the rats grow to the size of cats

article-025.text: Why does the writer explore old biological 'rules' alongside climate change?
options: To argue that future evolution is impossible to study.
To show that these rules have never been tested.
To suggest that evolutionary patterns can offer clues about how species may respond to warming.
To predict that every species will evolve in the same direction.
article-025.evidence: They also offer clues about how animals might adapt to a warming world

article-025.text: What is the point of the discussion of predators and prey evolving together?
options: An adaptation in one species may not improve its success if the species it depends on also changes.
Predators always become faster while prey remain unchanged.
Prey animals never respond to selection pressures.
Evolution guarantees that predators catch more food in every generation.
article-025.evidence: because the antelopes they hunt are also evolving to run faster, cheetahs don’t become more likely to catch the prey

article-025.text: How does the presence or absence of predators help explain size changes on islands?
options: Predators have no evolutionary effect on small animals.
All islands contain identical ecosystems.
Large animals can grow only when predators are abundant.
Reduced predation may allow small species to increase in size and compete more effectively.
article-025.evidence: Islands may also be free of predators, however, and some ecologists argue that this reduces the pressure on small animals to hide

article-025.text: What caution does the author express about forecasting evolution under climate change?
options: All organisms will change size at the same rate.
Evolutionary responses can vary even within one species, making simple universal predictions unreliable.
Scientists have concluded that climate has no influence on body size.
Every environmental change has one predictable biological consequence.
article-025.evidence: Even within a species, there may not be a uniform way of responding to climate change.

article-026.text: What ethical question lies at the centre of the article on biological computing?
options: Whether machines should be permitted to play video games.
Whether artificial intelligence should be banned from medical research.
At what point living brain-based computing systems might deserve consideration for their welfare.
Whether every organoid is identical to an adult human brain.
article-026.evidence: And at what point should we protect their welfare

article-026.text: Why does the writer describe experiments involving neural cells playing a simple game?
options: To illustrate that living neural systems may perform tasks usually associated with computing.
To prove that organoids possess all adult human emotions.
To claim ordinary silicon chips are made of living tissue.
To show that video games can cure brain diseases.
article-026.evidence: When they are in the game, they believe they are the paddle.

article-026.text: What practical scientific use of brain organoids does the article identify?
options: Replacing all animal populations with laboratory tissue.
Helping researchers investigate diseases of the brain.
Determining the outcomes of elections.
Eliminating the need for other forms of biological study.
article-026.evidence: researchers are creating more and more sophisticated brain organoids, mainly for studying brain diseases

article-026.text: Why is the writer reluctant to draw a fixed ethical boundary for biological AI?
options: The legal definition has already been settled worldwide.
All organoids demonstrably lack any response to stimulation.
Sentience is identical to performance on a computer test.
Current understanding of consciousness and feeling is too limited to make the distinction confidently.
article-026.evidence: we still don’t know enough about consciousness and feeling to be able to draw clear lines

article-026.text: What broader comparison does the author raise about welfare concerns?
options: Questions about the welfare of biological systems might also apply to future artificial systems based on silicon.
Only animal welfare matters, while all artificial systems are necessarily irrelevant.
Any machine that processes data is legally a human person.
Biological computing is guaranteed to replace every other form of AI.
article-026.evidence: Perhaps we should be worrying about the welfare of future Als just as much as we do about how Als will affect human welfare

article-027.text: How does the article apply Miyamoto Musashi's teachings to modern life?
options: As rules relevant only to historical sword fights.
As a collection of techniques for avoiding all personal responsibility.
As broader principles of personal discipline, clarity and self-reliance.
As proof that success depends entirely on luck.
article-027.evidence: these teachings have been applied in various contexts, including business and personal development

article-027.text: What does the writer suggest is the foundation of genuine self-discipline?
options: Focusing on essential responsibilities rather than only what feels pleasant.
Following every inherited custom without questioning it.
Seeking constant praise from others.
Avoiding tasks that require prolonged effort.
article-027.evidence: natural self-discipline springs from focusing on essential tasks, not merely pleasant

article-027.text: Why does the discussion warn against blind adherence to tradition?
options: Tradition makes all forms of learning impossible.
Independent understanding can help people make more deliberate and disciplined choices.
Every traditional practice is described as harmful.
It prevents students from respecting the past.
article-027.evidence: Breaking free from blind traditions allows us to act based on reason and understanding

article-027.text: What is implied by Musashi's advice to respect higher powers but take responsibility for one's actions?
options: People have no influence on the outcomes of their choices.
Others should always decide a person's direction.
Discipline relies chiefly on avoiding personal decisions.
Self-reliance requires recognising one's own role in shaping outcomes.
article-027.evidence: our actions determine our outcomes cultivates self-reliance and discipline

article-027.text: What overall message does the conclusion draw from Musashi's precepts?
options: Lasting self-discipline comes from internal principles and consistently following a chosen path.
Discipline can be achieved only through physical combat.
People should change their goals whenever they encounter resistance.
External symbols of success matter more than personal integrity.
article-027.evidence: Musashi’s 21 precepts serve as a timeless guide to self-discipline

article-028.text: Which quality does the article most strongly associate with Alexander's military success?
options: Reliance solely on numerical superiority.
Tactical adaptability and the ability to exploit his opponents' weaknesses.
A refusal to fight outside Macedonia.
Avoidance of all difficult terrain.
article-028.evidence: Alexander the Great of Macedonia was a unique tactician and general, undefeated in the field.

article-028.text: Why did Darius's numerical advantage not necessarily secure victory over Alexander?
options: His troops were prohibited from using weapons.
The opposing armies had agreed not to fight.
He was drawn into terrain that worked against his larger force.
He had refused to assemble any soldiers.
article-028.evidence: Darius, who believed he was chasing a retreating Macedonian army, was caught for battle in an area that heavily disadvantaged his larger force.

article-028.text: What does the account of the assault on the Sogdian Rock illustrate?
options: Alexander's forces sometimes used daring and difficult manoeuvres to overcome seemingly secure positions.
The Macedonians never fought in mountainous terrain.
All their victories were obtained by peaceful negotiation.
The fortress surrendered solely because of its food supplies.
article-028.evidence: At least 30 fell to their deaths, but in the morning, those who survived the climb signaled to Alexander from the top of the peak.

article-028.text: How does the account of Porus challenge the idea that every defeated ruler was permanently removed?
options: Porus never met Alexander during the campaigns.
Alexander abandoned India without fighting.
Porus led an uprising that ended Macedonian rule immediately.
Porus became a loyal ally after his confrontation with Alexander.
article-028.evidence: Porus remained a loyal ally of Alexander until the young Macedonian king’s death.

article-028.text: What does the selection of battles from Thebes to Gaugamela and beyond convey?
options: The campaign took place wholly within a single city.
Alexander's military operations spanned different regions and demanded varied approaches.
All the engagements involved the same opposing commander.
The article concerns only naval fighting.
article-028.evidence: From Thebes to Gaugamela and from there to the Sogdian Rock

article-029.text: What is the central focus of the interview with Ivor Perl?
options: A description of post-war technology.
A debate on how concentration camps were constructed.
A survivor's account of loss, survival and the lifelong task of living with those memories.
An argument that trauma always disappears after a few years.
article-029.evidence: At 12, I was in Auschwitz. My parents and seven siblings were murdered. Here is how I built a life

article-029.text: What is the significance of Perl's question about whether the world has learned anything from survivors?
options: It expresses concern that remembering atrocity should have consequences for how society behaves.
It means he wants every reader to agree about religion.
It denies that the Holocaust happened.
It suggests that personal testimonies cannot educate later generations.
article-029.evidence: is there anything the world has learned from us?

article-029.text: How does the interview describe the role of Perl's brother during his imprisonment?
options: His brother had no connection with his survival.
His brother repeatedly helped save his life under dangerous conditions.
They lived entirely separately and never met.
The interview suggests that surviving alone was an easy matter.
article-029.evidence: a number of times that he saved me literally from the jaws of death

article-029.text: What does the discussion of prisoners' limited knowledge of their fate reveal?
options: Every prisoner knew exactly what would happen upon arrival.
Historical testimony on this subject has been conclusively rejected.
People had unlimited access to outside news.
Fear, disbelief and lack of information could affect how victims understood their situation.
article-029.evidence: Jews not only had no inkling of the fate that awaited them when they arrived in Auschwitz

article-029.text: What does Perl's reaction to seeing young people at a campus illustrate?
options: His wartime memories remain emotionally present even decades after he built a new life.
Later generations always forget historical suffering.
He believes ordinary young people should be blamed for the Holocaust.
The passage says he has never spoken about his experiences.
article-029.evidence: I was their age when I was taken away. And my sisters, my mother. It always rears its head. You can never forget it.

article-030.text: Which question does the columnist identify as especially difficult to answer in science communication?
options: How to calculate everyday shopping prices.
How to distinguish classical mechanics from chemistry.
What existed before the universe began and what space-time actually means.
How to describe stars without using mathematics.
article-030.evidence: What was there before the beginning of the universe?

article-030.text: Why did Einstein's relativity challenge everyday assumptions about space and time?
options: The finite speed of light requires a different account of measurements made by moving observers.
It established that light's speed varies arbitrarily for each observer.
It proved distances can no longer be measured.
It removed all relationships between space and time.
article-030.evidence: Einstein’s relativity showed us that, in order to properly account for the finite speed of light, we could no longer think in these terms.

article-030.text: What does the article say about observers moving at different speeds?
options: One observer necessarily finds light to be stationary.
Each should measure the same speed of light even when their own motion differs.
Light travels only when the observer is at rest.
Their measurements are identical only if they are in the same place.
article-030.evidence: no matter what speed someone is moving, they have to measure the same speed of light

article-030.text: Why is the beginning of the universe a challenge for current physical explanations?
options: Astronomers have already watched the universe form.
The universe has no measurable properties.
Physical laws never change their mathematical form.
The equations become unreliable at time zero, limiting what can be inferred about an earlier state.
article-030.evidence: our equations become completely dysfunctional at time zero

article-030.text: What is the most defensible interpretation of the columnist's treatment of these questions?
options: They are profound questions whose answers require careful attention to the limits of present theories.
They are simple questions already resolved by common sense.
They are meaningless solely because the public asks them.
They can be answered without considering evidence or models.
article-030.evidence: there are two questions that I somewhat dread when communicating science to the public

article-031.text: What unusual characteristic distinguishes Triphyophyllum peltatum from other carnivorous plants described?
options: It eats insects throughout its entire life regardless of conditions.
It can become carnivorous only temporarily when certain nutrients are lacking.
It grows only in dry deserts rather than forests.
It catches prey exclusively with its roots.
article-031.evidence: the only one known to be a part-time carnivore

article-031.text: What did the controlled nutrient experiments identify as the trigger for carnivorous leaves?
options: A shortage of phosphorus.
A rise in air temperature alone.
An excess of potassium.
A lack of sunlight during the night.
article-031.evidence: Only plants starved of phosphorus grew carnivorous leaves.

article-031.text: Why did the researchers return some plants to ordinary growth medium?
options: To determine whether the roots would become permanently inactive.
To test whether the leaves would change colour.
To see whether removing the deficiency reversed the development of insect-trapping leaves.
To stop the plants from producing ordinary leaves.
article-031.evidence: new leaves emerged without the insect-trapping glands

article-031.text: What makes the results surprising in light of the researchers' expectations?
options: Carnivory was known to occur only in fully aquatic plants.
The leaves appeared only when plants received extra fertiliser.
The plant had never previously produced any unusual leaves.
The team expected nitrogen deficiency to matter more, but phosphorus deprivation proved decisive.
article-031.evidence: we and others were expecting nitrogen [deficiency] to be more likely

article-031.text: What survival advantage might temporary carnivory provide in the plant's native habitat?
options: It may help compensate for seasonal shortages of nutrients in shallow, acidic soils.
It allows the plant to stop depending on water.
It guarantees that other plants cannot grow nearby.
It eliminates the need for photosynthesis.
article-031.evidence: Carnivory may be an important survival mechanism in the plants’ native mountain slopes where the shallow, acidic soils become depleted of nutrients

article-032.text: Why did Costello the octopus attract the researchers' attention?
options: He was observed solving complex mathematical problems while awake.
He never showed any changes in behaviour.
He displayed sudden defensive-looking movements and released ink while apparently asleep.
He communicated with the researchers using written symbols.
article-032.evidence: he suddenly began thrashing around, tried to make himself look bigger by extending his mantle into a cone shape and released ink

article-032.text: What evidence suggests the episode was not entirely unique?
options: Researchers found several other, shorter episodes in many hours of recorded footage.
Every octopus in the aquarium displayed identical behaviour simultaneously.
Costello repeated the same event continuously for several days.
Similar episodes had been reported only in humans.
article-032.evidence: they found three similar, but shorter, events

article-032.text: Why do researchers compare certain octopus sleep phases with human REM sleep?
options: Octopuses become motionless and their eyes stop functioning permanently.
Changes in skin colour, eye movements and tentacle movements resemble activity seen during dreaming phases.
The phases last exactly the same length in every animal.
Octopus brain signals have already been proven identical to human dreams.
article-032.evidence: their eyes and tentacles move. This means it resembles the rapid eye movement (REM) sleep stage during which people dream.

article-032.text: What limitation prevents a firm conclusion that Costello experienced nightmares?
options: The recordings were made in daylight rather than darkness.
The researchers had never studied any octopus before.
A single event is sufficient to establish dreaming in all species.
There were few episodes in one animal, and alternative explanations such as parasomnia or ageing remain possible.
article-032.evidence: No conclusions can be drawn from a few episodes in one animal

article-032.text: What would the independent evolution of narrative dreams in cephalopods imply, according to Magnasco?
options: Dreaming could serve an important cognitive function in advanced brains.
Dreaming occurs only in mammals.
Octopuses have the same memories as human beings.
All sleeping animals must experience nightmares.
article-032.evidence: If narrative dreams have independently evolved in cephalopods, it suggests they are essential in advanced brains

article-033.text: What is the stated purpose of the article about Andrew Tate?
options: To present a legal account of all allegations against him.
To discuss perceived self-improvement themes in his message while acknowledging controversy.
To argue that personal growth should exclude physical fitness.
To claim that everyone agrees with his opinions.
article-033.evidence: While his views have stirred controversy, it is important to acknowledge the potential benefits of his empowering message.

article-033.text: What connection does the writer draw between exercise and personal development?
options: Exercise is unrelated to emotional wellbeing.
Fitness matters only for competitive athletes.
Regular activity can support physical health as well as confidence, focus and mental clarity.
Exercise removes the need for adequate sleep.
article-033.evidence: Regular exercise and fitness not only contribute to improved physical health but also enhance mental clarity, focus, and self-confidence.

article-033.text: How does the article frame the appeal of financial independence?
options: It can be associated with self-reliance and a greater sense of security.
It is possible only through illegal activity.
It is presented as a reason to avoid learning new skills.
